segments.narration: How fast is something moving at a single frozen moment in time? Motion requires time to pass — so the question sounds like nonsense. And yet, speedometers exist. That contradiction is exactly what we need to resolve.

Let's track the car. Every second, we mark how far it has traveled — and connect those dots into one smooth curve. This is the distance-versus-time graph. Now pick one moment we care about: call it point P.

Pick a second point Q a bit further along the curve. The line through P and Q is called a secant line — its slope is rise over run, delta-d over delta-t — which is just average speed over that little interval.
Now slide Q closer and closer to P. Watch the secant line rotate as the triangle shrinks — but notice the slope ratio settles toward a single value. It is converging.

In the limit, Q arrives at P — and the secant line becomes the tangent line, touching the curve at exactly one point. We never actually divide zero by zero; we ask what that slope ratio approaches. That limiting slope is the derivative.

Do this at every point on the curve and you get a brand new function — the derivative. One output per moment in time, each one telling you the instantaneous rate of change at that instant. Watch the slopes we found drop down and trace their own curve.

Instantaneous rate of change is not a contradiction — it is a limit. The derivative captures the best possible linear approximation at a single point. We started asking 'how fast at one instant?' — and now we have the answer: it is the slope of the tangent line, d-d over d-t, the derivative.
